title: Calamansi juice
intro: Freshly squeezed calamansi stretched with cold water and sweetened just enough to balance the sourness. It is bright, tart and very cold, the everyday juice for hot afternoons and for washing down fried food.

steps.text: Wash the calamansi and cut each one in half crosswise, just off center so most seeds stay in the smaller half.
Squeeze the halves over a small strainer set on a pitcher to catch the seeds. Squeeze firmly but do not twist the peel hard, or the juice turns bitter.
Stir the sugar into the warm water until it dissolves completely.
Add the syrup and cold water to the juice and stir. Taste and adjust with more sugar or water.
Fill glasses with ice and pour the juice over.

tips: The juice keeps for a day in a covered pitcher in the fridge. Add ice only to the glasses, never to the pitcher, so it does not get watery.

title: Salabat
intro: Fresh ginger simmered with brown sugar into a sweet, peppery hot drink. People drink it on cold mornings and rainy days, and at Christmas with puto bumbong or bibingka.

steps.text: Slice the ginger thinly, or smash it with the flat of a knife. There is no need to peel it if the skin is clean.
Put the ginger and water in a pot and bring to a boil.
Lower the heat, cover and simmer until the water is pale gold and tastes strongly of ginger.
Stir in the sugar and simmer until it dissolves. Taste and add more sugar if you like it sweeter.
Strain into cups and serve hot.

tips: For a stronger, spicier salabat, grate the ginger instead of slicing it and strain through a fine sieve. Leftovers keep for 3 days in the fridge; reheat without boiling hard.

title: Sago't gulaman
intro: Chewy sago pearls and cubes of gulaman in cold water sweetened with brown sugar syrup (arnibal). It tastes of caramel and vanilla, and it is the drink sold from big jars by street vendors on hot days.

items.name: drops red or brown food coloring

steps.text: Make the gulaman first. Sprinkle the gulaman powder over the water in a pot and stir. Bring to a boil, stirring, and boil until fully dissolved. Stir in the food coloring if using.
Pour into a square pan and leave to set at room temperature, or in the fridge to speed it up.

Meanwhile, bring the 6 cups of water to a rolling boil and add the sago. Simmer, stirring now and then so it does not stick, until the pearls are mostly clear with only a small white dot in the center.
Turn off the heat, cover the pot and let the sago stand until the white centers disappear.
Drain the sago and rinse it under cold water to wash off the starch.
For the arnibal, simmer the brown sugar, water and pandan in a small pan until slightly syrupy. Take off the heat, remove the pandan and stir in the vanilla.
Cut the set gulaman into small cubes.
In a pitcher, stir together the arnibal, cold water, sago and gulaman. Taste and add more water or syrup.
Serve over ice with wide straws or a long spoon.

tips: Cooked sago turns hard and white in the fridge, so keep it in the syrup mixture and finish the pitcher within a day. Ready-cooked sago from the market saves the boiling step.
